subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Every single day, from the moment you wake before Fajr to the moment you sleep at night, your body is quietly working. It is building new cells, repairing tissue, fighting illness, and giving you the energy to walk to school, help at home, play football, and think clearly in class. Where does all that energy and building material come from? It comes from the food you eat. In this unit you will discover the amazing journey that a plate of bariis (rice) with fish, or a piece of canjeero with a cup of camel milk, takes as it travels through your body.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, experiments and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Identify the constituents of a balanced diet for humans as including protein, carbohydrates, fats and oils, water, minerals (limited to calcium and iron) and vitamins (limited to A, C and D), and describe the functions of these nutrients.
Understand that carbohydrates and fats can be used as a store of energy in animals, and animals consume food to obtain energy and nutrients.
Discuss how human growth, development and health can be affected by lifestyle, including diet and smoking.
Identify ball-and-socket and hinge joints, and explain how antagonistic muscles move the bones at a hinge joint.

Describe the components of blood and their functions (limited to red blood cells transporting oxygen, white blood cells protecting against pathogens and plasma transporting blood cells, nutrients and carbon dioxide).

Describe how the structure of the human respiratory system is related to its function of gas exchange (in terms of lung structure and the action of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles) and understand the difference between breathing and respiration.
Describe the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and the air in the lungs.
Collect and record sufficient observations and/or measurements in an appropriate form.

objectives.subStrand: Scientific enquiry: analysis, evaluation and conclusions
objectives.text: Present and interpret observations and measurements appropriately.

outcomes: Name the main food groups and nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins, minerals, water and fibre - and give a local food example of each.
Explain the job of each nutrient in the body and describe what happens when a nutrient is missing (deficiency).
Describe a balanced diet and explain why different people (a farmer, a baby, a pregnant mother, a person fasting) need different amounts of food.
Name the organs of the digestive system in order and state the function of each: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and the helper organs (liver, pancreas).
Explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion and give an example of each.
Describe what enzymes are and explain how they break large food molecules into small, soluble ones.
Explain absorption - how digested food passes into the blood through the wall of the small intestine.
Carry out simple food tests for starch, sugar and fat, and interpret the results.
Apply your knowledge to plan a healthy, balanced meal from foods available in your community.
Learn these words well. They are the tools you will use to think and write about food and digestion.

concepts.title: Why Does Your Body Need Food?
concepts.explanation:
Think about a car or a lorry travelling on the road from Hargeisa to Berbera. It cannot move without fuel. Your body is far more wonderful than any machine, but it too needs fuel and building materials. Food does three great jobs in your body:

It gives you energy. Every movement — running, breathing, even blinking — uses energy. Your body also uses energy just to stay warm and keep your heart beating. This energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and fats.

It helps you grow and repair. You are still growing! Your body builds new cells and heals wounds using proteins and minerals. When Amina cuts her finger, her body repairs the skin using material from the food she eats.

It keeps you healthy and protected. Vitamins and minerals keep your eyes, skin, bones and blood working well and help you fight off illness such as malaria or infections.

Because food does so many different jobs, no single food can do everything. Rice alone gives energy but cannot build strong muscles. Meat alone builds muscle but gives little quick energy. This is exactly why we need a balanced diet — a mixture of many foods.
concepts.example: Did You Know? An active 12-year-old needs roughly 2000 to 2200 kilojoules of energy from food per day — and even more if you walk long distances to school or help herd goats. When you are asleep, your body still uses about one-fifth of its daytime energy just to keep you alive.

concepts.title: The Nutrients In Your Food
concepts.explanation:
Scientists group the substances in food into seven types of nutrient. Let us look at each one, its job, and where you can find it in the foods around you.

Carbohydrates are your body's main and fastest source of energy. There are two kinds: starch and sugars. Starchy foods release their energy slowly and steadily, which is why a plate of bariis or canjeero keeps you going for hours. Sugars release energy very quickly but do not last long. A date gives you a quick burst of energy — which is one reason the Prophet (peace be upon him) recommended breaking the fast with dates at iftar. Good sources include rice, canjeero, pasta, potatoes, sweet potatoes, bread, dates and honey.

Proteins are the building blocks of your body. Your muscles, skin, hair and even your blood are made largely of protein. Growing children, pregnant mothers and people healing from illness need plenty of protein. Proteins come from two places: animal sources such as fish from the Indian Ocean, goat meat, camel milk, eggs and cheese; and plant sources such as beans, lentils and groundnuts. A meal of beans (digir) is an excellent and affordable way to get protein.

Fats and oils (lipids) — the energy stores

Fats give more energy per gram than any other nutrient — more than twice as much as carbohydrate. Your body stores extra fat under the skin, where it also keeps you warm. Fats are found in cooking oil, ghee (subag), the fat on meat, milk, nuts and avocado. You need some fat, but too much — especially from fried and oily foods — can be harmful over time, so eat fats in moderation.

Vitamins are needed only in very small amounts, but without them the body cannot work properly. For example, vitamin C (found in mango, lime, guava and tomatoes) keeps your gums and skin healthy and helps wounds heal. Vitamin A (found in liver, milk, and orange vegetables like carrots and pumpkin) keeps your eyes healthy, especially your ability to see in dim light. Vitamin D, which your skin makes in sunlight, helps build strong bones — and in sunny East Africa, that vitamin is a daily gift.

Minerals are simple substances the body needs in small amounts. Calcium (in milk, cheese and small fish eaten with bones) builds strong bones and teeth. Iron (in red meat, liver, beans and dark green leaves) is needed to make healthy red blood. A person who lacks iron becomes tired and pale — a condition called anaemia, which is common and can be prevented by eating iron-rich foods.

More than half of your body is water. You need water for your blood, for digestion, for sweating to keep cool in the heat, and for removing waste in urine. In a hot, sometimes dry climate, and especially when you are fasting, drinking enough clean water is very important. Always drink water that is safe — from a protected well, or boiled and cooled — to avoid diseases like cholera and diarrhoea.

Fibre is the tough part of plant foods that your body cannot digest, such as the skins of beans and vegetables and the outer part of whole grains. Even though it is not absorbed, fibre is very important: it gives the muscles of your gut something to push against, keeping food moving smoothly and preventing constipation. Vegetables, fruit, beans and whole grains are all rich in fibre.
concepts.example: When a nutrient is missing from the diet for a long time, the body suffers a deficiency. Each missing nutrient causes its own problem. Too little protein slows growth and weakens the muscles, which is serious for growing children. Too little iron causes anaemia, leaving a person tired and pale. Too little vitamin C causes scurvy, where the gums bleed and wounds heal slowly. Too little vitamin A can harm the eyes and make it hard to see in dim light. Too little calcium or vitamin D leaves bones weak and soft. This is the strongest reason of all to eat a varied, balanced diet: each food brings something the others cannot, and together they keep every part of you healthy.

concepts.title: A Balanced Diet
concepts.explanation:
A balanced diet contains all seven nutrients in the correct amounts. Picture a plate. Roughly, a healthy plate should have a good portion of carbohydrate (rice, canjeero or potato) for energy, a portion of protein (fish, meat or beans) for growth, plenty of vegetables and fruit for vitamins, minerals and fibre, a small amount of fat, and always a drink of clean water. A meal of bariis with fish, a spoon of vegetables, and a mango afterwards is close to a perfectly balanced plate.

Not everyone needs the same amount of food. The amount depends on several things:

Age: A growing teenager needs more protein for building than an elderly person. A baby needs milk above all.

Activity: A fisherman rowing all day, or a boy herding goats across the savanna, needs far more energy than someone sitting most of the day.

Body size: A larger body needs more food to run it.

Special conditions: A pregnant mother eats for herself and her growing baby, so she needs extra protein, iron and calcium.

Too little food of the right kind leads to malnutrition — the body becomes weak, growth slows, and illness comes easily. Too much food, especially too much sugar and fat, can lead to being overweight and to health problems later in life. Balance is the goal in all things.

Did You Know? Eating too much sugar does not only cause tooth decay. Over many years, a diet very high in sugar can lead to a serious illness called type 2 diabetes, where the body can no longer control the sugar level in the blood. Choosing fruit and dates for sweetness, instead of many sweets and sugary drinks, protects your future health.
concepts.example: During Ramadan, when many Muslims fast from dawn to sunset, a balanced diet becomes even more important. At suhoor (the meal before dawn), foods that release energy slowly — like whole grains, beans, and canjeero — help you feel full and strong through the day. Plenty of water at suhoor helps you stay hydrated. At iftar, breaking the fast gently with dates and water, then eating a balanced meal, is both a beautiful tradition and wise nutrition. Eating well during Ramadan lets you worship and study with strength.

concepts.title: The Journey Through Your Digestive System
concepts.explanation:
Now for the amazing journey. The food you eat is far too big and complex to enter your blood as it is. A grain of rice cannot simply slip into your bloodstream! It must first be broken down into tiny, soluble molecules. This breaking-down process is called digestion, and it happens along a long muscular tube called the digestive system (or alimentary canal). If you could stretch this tube out straight, it would be several metres long — longer than you are tall, coiled neatly inside you.

Let us follow a piece of canjeero on its journey, organ by organ. Imagine the path as a long, winding road, and each organ is a station where a different job is done.

Digestion begins the moment you take a bite. Your teeth cut and grind the food into smaller pieces. This is mechanical digestion — physically breaking food apart, like using a pestle and mortar. At the same time, glands in your mouth release saliva. Saliva makes the food soft and slippery, and it contains an enzyme called amylase that begins chemical digestion by starting to break starch down into sugar. This is why, if you chew a piece of plain canjeero or bread for a long time, it slowly begins to taste slightly sweet — the amylase is turning starch into sugar right there in your mouth. Your tongue then rolls the food into a soft ball and pushes it to the back of your throat to be swallowed.

When you swallow, the ball of food enters the oesophagus (the gullet), a muscular tube that connects your mouth to your stomach. Food does not simply fall down by gravity — if it did, you could not eat lying down or drink while bending over. Instead, the muscles in the wall of the oesophagus squeeze in waves behind the food, pushing it along. This wave-like squeezing is called peristalsis, and it happens all the way along your gut.

The oesophagus leads to the stomach, a stretchy, muscular bag. Here the food stays for a few hours. The stomach walls churn and squeeze the food, mixing it thoroughly — more mechanical digestion. The stomach also releases gastric juice, which contains a strong acid (hydrochloric acid) and enzymes that begin to digest proteins. The acid has a second important job: it kills most of the harmful germs (bacteria) that may have come in with the food, protecting you from illness. After a few hours, the food has become a thick, souplike liquid.

4. The small intestine — where most digestion and absorption happen

The soupy food now passes into the small intestine, a long, narrow, coiled tube where the most important work happens. It is called 'small' because it is narrow, but it is actually the longest part of the gut — about six metres in an adult. Here, digestive juices from the pancreas and liver pour in and mix with the food. Enzymes finish breaking down carbohydrates, proteins and fats into their smallest molecules: carbohydrates into glucose (a simple sugar), proteins into amino acids, and fats into fatty acids. The liver makes a green-yellow liquid called bile, stored in the gall bladder, which breaks large drops of fat into tiny droplets so the enzymes can work on them more easily.

Once the food is fully digested into these tiny soluble molecules, they are ready to be absorbed — to pass through the wall of the small intestine and into the blood. The inside wall of the small intestine is not smooth; it is covered with millions of tiny finger-like folds called villi (one is a villus). These villi give the wall a huge surface area, like the many tiny loops of a towel that soak up much more water than a flat cloth. Because of this enormous surface, digested food is absorbed quickly and efficiently into the blood, which carries the nutrients to every cell in your body.

So what is blood, and what else does it carry? A little over half of it is plasma, a straw-coloured liquid that carries the dissolved nutrients you have just absorbed, along with wastes and heat. Floating in that plasma are three kinds of cell, each with its own job. Red blood cells are packed with a red pigment called haemoglobin, which grips oxygen and carries it to every working cell. White blood cells are part of your defence against infection. Platelets are cell fragments that clump together to seal a cut — they are why Amina's finger stops bleeding.

The oxygen those red cells carry is collected in your lungs. Each lung divides into finer and finer tubes that end in millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli. The trick is the one the small intestine already showed you: an enormous surface area folded into a small space. The wall of an alveolus is a single cell thick and is wrapped in blood capillaries whose walls are also a single cell thick, so the air and the blood are separated by almost nothing.

Gases cross that thin barrier by diffusion, moving from where they are crowded to where they are not. The air in an alveolus is rich in oxygen and the blood arriving there is poor in it, so oxygen diffuses into the blood. Carbon dioxide, the waste your cells produce, is crowded in the arriving blood and scarce in the air, so it diffuses the other way and you breathe it out.
concepts.example: By now, almost all the useful nutrients have been absorbed. What remains is the material the body cannot digest — mainly fibre and water. This passes into the large intestine. Here, most of the water is absorbed back into the body, so the body does not waste it. This is why drinking enough water matters: some of the water your gut uses is reclaimed here. The remaining solid waste, called faeces, is stored until it leaves the body through the anus. If a person has diarrhoea, water is not properly reabsorbed and is lost from the body, which is why diarrhoea can cause dangerous dehydration — and why drinking clean water and salts to replace the loss is so important.

concepts.title: Mechanical and Chemical Digestion
concepts.explanation:
Digestion happens in two ways that work together, and it is important to tell them apart.

Mechanical digestion is the physical breaking of food into smaller pieces without changing what it is made of. Your teeth grinding food and your stomach churning it are both mechanical. Think of breaking a large loaf into crumbs — the crumbs are still bread. Mechanical digestion is helpful because it creates many smaller pieces, giving the enzymes a much larger surface to work on.

Chemical digestion is the breaking of large food molecules into small ones using enzymes and other chemicals like acid and bile. This actually changes the food into different, simpler substances — starch becomes sugar, protein becomes amino acids. Chemical digestion happens in the mouth (starch), the stomach (protein), and the small intestine (all nutrients).

The two work as a team. Mechanical digestion breaks the food into small pieces so that chemical digestion, using enzymes, can act on a large surface and finish the job quickly. If you swallowed food without chewing, the enzymes would have far less surface to work on and digestion would be slow and difficult. This is also why we are taught to eat calmly and chew our food well.

None of that chewing would happen without the machinery that moves your jaw. Bones themselves cannot bend, so wherever the body needs to move, two bones meet at a joint. Your jaw swings on a hinge joint, which opens and closes in one plane like a door; your elbow and knee are hinges too. A ball-and-socket joint, where the rounded end of one bone sits in a cup in another, turns in almost any direction — that is your shoulder and your hip. It is why you can swing your arm in a full circle but bend your elbow only one way.

Muscles move those bones, and there is a catch: a muscle can only pull, never push. So muscles are arranged in antagonistic pairs that pull in opposite directions. At the elbow, the biceps on top of your upper arm contracts and shortens to bend the joint while the triceps underneath relaxes; to straighten the arm again the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. Your jaw works the same way — one set of muscles contracts to close it against the food, another set opens it again — and those two take turns for every mouthful you chew.
concepts.example: Yes — it becomes a new, simpler substance.

concepts.title: Enzymes, The Tiny Workers
concepts.explanation:
Enzymes are one of the most wonderful discoveries in biology. An enzyme is a special kind of protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up itself. Because they speed things up, we call them biological catalysts. Without enzymes, digesting a single meal might take days or even weeks. With them, it takes only hours.

A useful way to picture an enzyme is a key and lock. Each enzyme has a special shape that fits only one type of food molecule, just as one key fits only one lock. When the food molecule fits into the enzyme, the enzyme snips it apart into smaller pieces. Then the enzyme is free to grab the next molecule and do it again, and again, thousands of times.

There are three main groups of digestive enzymes you should know:

Carbohydrase (for example, amylase) breaks carbohydrates (starch) into sugars (glucose). It works in the mouth and small intestine.

Protease breaks proteins into amino acids. It works in the stomach and small intestine.

Lipase breaks fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol. It works in the small intestine.

Enzymes are fussy about their conditions. They work best at your body temperature, about 37 degrees Celsius — which is one reason your body keeps itself warm. They also each need the right level of acid: the protease in your stomach likes acidic conditions, while the enzymes in the small intestine prefer conditions that are slightly alkaline. If an enzyme gets too hot, its special shape is destroyed forever — we say it is denatured — and it can no longer work, like a key that has been melted out of shape.
concepts.example: Did You Know? Enzymes are not only inside your body. The same kind of enzymes are used in washing powders to break down food and grease stains on clothes, and in making cheese from milk. When you help wash clothes at home with enzyme washing powder, you are using biology!

methods.title: Testing Foods For Starch
methods.example: To find out which local foods contain starch, using iodine solution as the test.
steps: Wash your hands and lay out a small piece of each food in its own spot on the plate.
Add one or two drops of iodine solution onto each food.
Watch carefully for about 30 seconds. A blue-black colour means starch is present. If the iodine stays its normal brown-orange colour, there is no starch.
Record the colour for each food in the table below.
Observation Table

methods.title: The Fat Test With Paper
methods.example: To find out which foods contain fat (lipid), using the grease-spot test on paper.
steps: Draw and label a small circle on the paper for each food.
Rub a little of each food onto its circle. For water, put one drop.
Leave the paper in a warm, airy place for about 15 minutes so any water dries.
Hold the paper up to the light. A translucent (see-through) greasy spot that does NOT dry away means the food contains fat. The water spot will dry and leave no permanent mark.
Record your results.

methods.title: Modelling Mechanical Digestion And Surface Area
methods.example: To show why chewing (mechanical digestion) speeds up chemical digestion, by seeing how surface area affects how fast something dissolves.
steps: Fill both glasses with the same amount of water at the same temperature.
Into glass A, add the whole lump of sugar. Into glass B, add the crushed sugar. Do not stir.
Watch and time how long each takes to dissolve completely.
Record the times.
Observation Table

methods.title: Planning And Investigating A Balanced Plate
methods.example: To investigate the meals eaten in your home for one day and design a balanced plate.
steps: For one day, write down every food eaten at each meal in your home.
For each food, decide which nutrient group(s) it mainly provides.
Fill in the record sheet below, ticking which nutrients appeared.
Look for any nutrient group that was missing or eaten very little.
Design an improved balanced plate that fills the gap using local, affordable foods.

workedExamples.title: Planning A Balanced Plate
workedExamples.prompt: Let us plan a balanced lunch for Maryam, a 12-year-old who walks to school and plays outside. We will check that every nutrient group is included.
workedExamples.solution:
Step 1 — Start with energy (carbohydrate). Maryam is active, so she needs good energy. We choose a portion of bariis (rice). This supplies starch for steady energy.

Step 2 — Add growth food (protein). She is still growing, so she needs protein. We add a piece of grilled fish from the coast, or a serving of beans if fish is not available.

Step 3 — Add vitamins, minerals and fibre. We add a spoonful of cooked vegetables (such as spinach or carrots) and a fresh mango for vitamin C and fibre.

Step 4 — Include a little fat. The fish is cooked with a small amount of oil, which supplies fat — but we keep it modest.

activities.title: Testing Foods For Starch
activities.materials: Iodine solution (from a pharmacy; the type used to clean wounds works, but ask an adult).; Small pieces of several foods: cooked rice, canjeero or bread, raw potato, a slice of banana, a little cooking oil, a little sugar, a piece of mango.; A clean white plate or several small saucers.; A dropper or a clean teaspoon; paper towel; water for cleaning.
steps: Wash your hands and lay out a small piece of each food in its own spot on the plate.
Add one or two drops of iodine solution onto each food.
Watch carefully for about 30 seconds. A blue-black colour means starch is present. If the iodine stays its normal brown-orange colour, there is no starch.
Record the colour for each food in the table below.
Observation Table

activities.title: The Fat Test With Paper
activities.materials: Plain paper (brown paper or a page of a notebook works well).; Small amounts of: cooking oil, ghee (subag) or butter, a groundnut (peanut), a piece of avocado, a drop of water (for comparison), a little sugar.; A pencil to label; a warm sunny spot or a windowsill.
steps: Draw and label a small circle on the paper for each food.
Rub a little of each food onto its circle. For water, put one drop.
Leave the paper in a warm, airy place for about 15 minutes so any water dries.
Hold the paper up to the light. A translucent (see-through) greasy spot that does NOT dry away means the food contains fat. The water spot will dry and leave no permanent mark.
Record your results.

activities.title: Modelling Mechanical Digestion And Surface Area
activities.materials: Two clear glasses of water at the same temperature.; Two equal amounts of sugar (or two sugar cubes if you have them): one left whole/in a lump, one crushed or ground.; A spoon; a clock or phone to time.
steps: Fill both glasses with the same amount of water at the same temperature.
Into glass A, add the whole lump of sugar. Into glass B, add the crushed sugar. Do not stir.
Watch and time how long each takes to dissolve completely.
Record the times.
Observation Table

activities.title: Planning And Investigating A Balanced Plate
activities.materials: A notebook and pencil.; Access to observe (with permission) the meals eaten in your home for one day.; The nutrient list from your Lesson file.
steps: For one day, write down every food eaten at each meal in your home.
For each food, decide which nutrient group(s) it mainly provides.
Fill in the record sheet below, ticking which nutrients appeared.
Look for any nutrient group that was missing or eaten very little.
Design an improved balanced plate that fills the gap using local, affordable foods.

realProblems.answer: Boiling water kills the harmful germs (bacteria) that cause diseases such as cholera and diarrhoea, protecting the gut and preventing dehydration and illness.

realProblems.prompt: A young child in the community is tired and pale. Which mineral might be lacking, which foods would help, and what is the condition called?
realProblems.answer: The child may lack the mineral iron; iron-rich foods such as red meat, liver, beans and dark green leaves would help. The condition of tiredness and paleness from too little iron is called anaemia.

realProblems.prompt: Explain, step by step, how a mouthful of fish is digested and absorbed, naming the organs, the enzyme group involved, and the final products.
realProblems.answer: In the mouth the fish is chewed (mechanical). It passes down the oesophagus by peristalsis to the stomach, where acid and protease begin digesting the protein and germs are killed. In the small intestine, protease (with juices from the pancreas) finishes breaking the protein into amino acids. The amino acids are absorbed through the villi into the blood and carried to the cells for growth and repair.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Name the seven types of nutrient the body needs.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: State the main job of proteins in the body and give one local source.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Proteins build and repair body cells and tissues (growth). Local source: fish, goat meat, camel milk, or beans.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion in one sentence each.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Mechanical digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces (e.g. chewing). Chemical digestion breaks large molecules into small ones using enzymes (e.g. amylase turning starch to sugar).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: List, in order, the five main organs food passes through from the mouth to the anus.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine (then out through the anus).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: What is an enzyme? Why is it called a biological catalyst?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: An enzyme is a special protein that speeds up the breaking down of food. It is a biological catalyst because it speeds up a reaction without being used up itself.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain what 'absorption' means and where it mainly happens.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Absorption is the passing of digested food from the gut into the blood. It happens mainly in the small intestine through the villi.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is NOT digested by the body but keeps the gut moving?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 7 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: fibre — fibre is not digested but keeps the gut moving.

rounds.prompt: Which nutrient is the body's main and fastest source of energy?
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 7 Science Words reference.
rounds.explanation: carbohydrate — carbohydrates give the fastest, main energy supply.

rounds.prompt: The wave-like squeezing that pushes food along the gut is called:

selfAssessment: I can name the main food groups and nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats (lipids), vitamins, minerals, water and fibre - and give a local food example of each.
I can explain the job of each nutrient in the body and describe what happens when a nutrient is missing (deficiency).
I can describe a balanced diet and explain why different people (a farmer, a baby, a pregnant mother, a person fasting) need different amounts of food.
I can name the organs of the digestive system in order and state the function of each: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and the helper organs (liver, pancreas).
I can explain the difference between mechanical and chemical digestion and give an example of each.
I can describe what enzymes are and explain how they break large food molecules into small, soluble ones.
I can explain absorption - how digested food passes into the blood through the wall of the small intestine.
I can carry out simple food tests for starch, sugar and fat, and interpret the results.
